Before you give your answer, on the 24th of May, 1995, there was this meeting and we see that Mr. Stojic, who is the assistant to the minister in charge of personnel affairs, and I see that at this meeting there is also Zeljko Siljeg, who is a brigadier. He was promoted, so Siljeg was promoted while Mr. Stojic is the assistant to the minister. Is this a conventional way of doing things? What do you say about this? If you don't know, just say you don't know and I'll stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, I can't really say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Go on Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have 12 minutes left, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can now look at P 10783. Now, sir, this is a document signed by Bruno Stojic, and it says assistant minister for personnel, and it is dated 11 July 1995. And it's addressed to the Ministry of Defence, Security and Information Service Administration, personally to Mr. Zvonko Sesar, and it's in response to a letter by him. It says: "Pursuant to your letter to this administration mentioned above in which you had requested us to send you all available information on Mr. Ivica Rajic, we would like to inform you as follows ..." Now, my first question to you, sir, is: In 1995, did you know who Ivica Rajic was, you personally?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Certain you had heard of the events that took place in Stupni Do in 1993, towards the end, October 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just through the media, media speculation, otherwise nothing official.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And in the media speculation, wasn't the name of Ivica Rajic mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear of that. Events were mentioned, but as to names, I didn't hear any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, regardless of that, if we look at the information contained in this, it gives basically three bits, four bits of information. It says Mr. Rajic was born in 1958 and he was registered with Kiseljak Defence Department. He performed the following duties, and then it says he was intelligence advisor at north-west Herzegovina pursuant to the order of Mr. Bruno Stojic. If we turn over it says he was commander of Kiseljak, Ban Jelacic, dismissed from that position by order of Mate Boban dated 15 January 1993. And then it is pretty silent on what happens then apart from saying in the final paragraph it should be noted that the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban, has presented Ivica Rajic with a decree, with a number, dated 1 November 1993, granting him an active colonel's rank. Now, sir, in view of the fact that Mr. Rajic was still in the HVO during -- or after the period of January 1993, and he was involved in a command role in the events of Stupni Do which you had heard about in the media, it's clear that the information in this letter isn't complete. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see nothing contentious there, from the dates, the appointments, the duties. So that's something that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, does this document say anything about the service of Mr. -- or rather, I shall put it to you, it doesn't say anything really about the service of Mr. Rajic from January 1993, through the rest of 1993, except that he was awarded the rank of colonel?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any explanations there except that the positions he occupied are set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether there was a -- I think I'll leave that -- that there. I don't think you'll be able to help us further on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my examination. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, I would like to say the following: It would have been interesting to have the letter from Mr. Zvonko Sesar, who is responsible for the SIS at the Ministry of Defence, the letter that he sent to Mr. Stojic on July 6. What did that letter request? Was he asking for information about what Rajic was doing during the year 1993, or was he asking something else? We don't really know what was asked in that letter. That could perhaps explain the elements that are missing in this text. Perhaps in your archives you could find that letter dated July 6th. Well, now, Madam Nozica, I'm certain you have some additional questions, but before that, Witness, I have a question. Could you take a look at the map which is on the second to the last page of the Prosecutor's binder. Where we have all those red dots. And you can see that it's almost 100 per cent Croatian in this zone, and around Mostar as well. According to your knowledge, and of course I'm only asking you to respond if you know this, what is the historical reason which would explain the fact that the Croatians assembled in this zone that can be seen on the map around Citluk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know except to say that I was born as a Croat in Citluk, but as to historical reasons, I really can't address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know why? Well, one more question. Yesterday Mr. Kruger asked you a question about the Muslims in Citluk who were imprisoned. It seems that in 1991 there were 111 Muslims and, therefore, I am assuming that in 1992, 1993, the number might have been slightly higher or around the same. Amongst those individuals there were women, children, grandparents, that included everyone. So if you divide by two, let's say there were at the most 50 men, but if you remove the age group under 18, under 17, and then the elderly men over the age of 60, that leaves you with a fairly small number. You weren't very clear in your answers. According to your knowledge, were there many Muslims, and I'm being very careful in the words I use, were there many Muslims who were displaced, arrested, imprisoned, to your knowledge, were there a number of Muslims who ended up in a place where they were no longer free to come and go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have understood your question and I'll repeat what I know, and I ought to know a great deal or quite a lot, that there was no restriction of freedoms or arrests, and as far as I know, most of those people stayed on in the Citluk region and continued to live there. From my experience, I know a particular situation in a small village where I personally sought protection for part of the population there to avoid any retaliation or revenge because a couple of young guys were killed in the space of a few days and one of them was an only child, an only son. So although the situation was tense, it was resolved successfully. So I really think that as far as Citluk is concerned, and especially the office, there were never any complaints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you. Madam Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will be brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, you were referring to a situation in a particular village, and as far as I understood you, you said that potentially there could be problems with some Muslims and then you intervened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Nozica, in your supplementary questions, in keeping with directive 3, paragraph 9, there -- you have two hours. You've used those two hours, so the time that you are using now will be deducted from your overall credit of time, the time you are using for this re-examination. You do understand that?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have major problems with that, but I have to agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mentioned a place near Citluk a moment ago where you intervened because of the potential chance of somebody attacking some Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, for the record, would you just tell us what the name of that village was and when that happened?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but I know that it was the village of Krucevici and that it was a village with a mixed population. Although it was a small village, nonetheless, the inhabitants were ethnically mixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So it is Krucevici, the name of the village, right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krucevici.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We'll -- it will be seen in the transcript and I'll see to the proper spelling of the place with the court reporter later on. Now, Judge Antonetti asked you how come that around Citluk, in that area, whether you knew that it was mostly inhabited by Croats, historically speaking. Now, this brought a question to mind, if you can answer it, fine; if not it doesn't matter, but I think it is common knowledge, and it is this: In certain areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina before this war, were there large areas in which the Muslims were the prevailing inhabitants almost 100 per cent and other villages and areas which were almost 100 per cent inhabited by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any large areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well let's take Cazinska Krajina for instance?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Muslims. Muslim inhabited.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, I'm appealing to your knowledge as a teacher here because you were a teacher, were you not. Now in Cazinski -- in the Cazin area, which is rather a large area, wasn't it inhabited 100 per cent by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether 100 per cent, but I do know that up there in that area there are Croats too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, I said almost 100 per cent?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, in the Romanija area and in eastern Herzegovina, are there areas of similar size, like Citluk and Citluk municipality, which were inhabited almost 100 per cent by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, I'd like to go back to a question that you were asked by Judge Antonetti earlier on about the invitational summons. And could you take a look at the document once again, or perhaps you don't have to, but the document is P 4646, and let me remind you, perhaps we have it on e-court, P 4646, it is the invitation sent -- I'm not going to deal with the contents of the document. This is an invitation signed by Mr. Stojic and sent to Major-General Slobodan Praljak; right?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, take a look at document P 4756. And it is the minutes dated the 2nd of October, 1993. And look at that first sentence there and we see that instead of the commander of the HVO, it was the deputy chief who was present, and on page 2 we see that that was Mr. Matic who was the deputy of the Chief of the Main Staff. Now, within the frameworks of the question asked by Judge Antonetti as to whether this was a summons or an invitation, from these two documents can we see that Mr. Praljak didn't respond to the invitation to the meeting, and I believe that it was for justified reasons. Let's not go into that here, not the reasons.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And finally Mr. Pinjuh, you said several times that you were at a -- employed at a low level. Let's see how low that level is in which you were. If we look at the Defence Department, now, the defence office, is that the lowest administrative level within the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, Mr. Pinjuh, you were shown a series of documents, orders, and so on. You were asked to comment on some rules and regulations. Did you say that you couldn't comment on them because you knew nothing about them because the level was high, high above your level, or because simply you didn't want to comment, you didn't wish to comment, which was it?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said everything I knew. Whenever I knew the answer, I gave it, but when I didn't know the answer, that's what I said. And that's what the case was, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Pinjuh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Your Honours, that completes my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, sir, on behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for having come to testify for the Defence of Mr. Stojic. I would like to wish you a safe trip home and I would like to ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Nozica, I wanted to say the following: We've received the schedule for the next weeks that you sent us and I'd like to tell you right away that you had scheduled something for April 30th, Mr. Bagaric at 4.00 -- or sorry, for four hours, but that is United Nations holiday on April 30th, so there will be no court session, so you'll have to reschedule that one. We won't be able to finish four hours in three days so we'll have to think about that. I'd like to also add that several witnesses are scheduled for one hour, March 11th there's Bahto, and then on the 12th, Cengic. There's also April 1st, Prelic; and April 2nd, Mandic; April 8th, Korac; and April 9th, Kresic. Now, that's all fine, however, you must also take account of the fact that if we finish Bahto on the 11th, the 11 of March, that we be able to begin Cengic right away. So please do schedule these things in such a way so that if you only have -- if you only need an hour, that you be able to continue with the next witness. I am assuming this is not going to be a major problem for you, but it would be a good thing if you could do that. Aside from that, at this point in time, I don't have anything else to say to you, but for the witnesses that are only coming for one hour, please do schedule them closer together. For example, tomorrow we have a one-hour witness. If he had been here already, we could have continued this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will bear that in mind. I'll take care of it. I have been very careful not to waste hours in the courtroom, but I also have a problem with the witnesses. These are people who have their work to do. It was very hard for me to harmonize my agenda and my schedule with theirs. I can't keep them here waiting for three or four days. The next witness who is entering the courtroom tomorrow is the chief of a large clinic in Mostar. I couldn't ask him to come here on Thursday or Friday for proofing. We are having serious problems with that. But as for us in the Defence, we will certainly take care that time is not wasted. However, Your Honours must bear in mind that we must also take into account what our witnesses can do. Sometimes there's nothing we can do about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. All of your witnesses are not the directors of clinics. Perhaps it's easier for some of them and perhaps amongst the witnesses they might -- some of them might be happy to come here. So it's up to you to work it out. Yes, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm grateful for the indulgence allowing us to file our response to the Prosecution's motion regarding Dragan Pinjuh tomorrow morning and we will file tomorrow morning. I make a related application, the practice direction limits, ordinarily, responses to 3.000 words. At the moment we require 3.800 words. I have communicated with the good officers of the case manager, Ms. Winner, with Mr. Scott and there's no objection, very kindly from the Prosecution, if we are granted by Your Honours an additional 800 words to file our response, and that is my application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber grants that request. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, just a brief submission. It won't take longer than two minutes, perhaps. Recently there have been some issues concerning my client, and you mentioned more than once that you would ask General Praljak about these things when he testifies. This happened again today. I discussed this topic with General Praljak more than once and an idea came up during our conversations which I will propose to you now. It may not be orthodox, but I don't see that it goes against the rules, and I believe it could certainly contribute to the efficiency of the trial. The idea was the following: There are occasions when it would be useful and practical to hear the response of one of the accused, to hear his testimony right away. Of course, the testimony of the accused has to take a certain form, starting with the solemn declaration. But my proposal is as follows: My client is fully prepared, at your request, when there is a question you wish to put to him, to give a precise response to the best of his recollection. Of course, he is willing to make a solemn declaration which will apply to each such response, a blanket declaration covering all such instances. It would often be really useful if there is a question about a document or a detail cropping up during witness testimony to put a question to the accused who is responding as the accused testifying under oath. And then that would assist the Chamber when putting questions to that witness or other witnesses. This is our proposal which we see as being useful, conducive to expeditiousness and saving time, and also dealing with a topic or an issue as it crops up in the courtroom while it is still of interest and topical. If you so wish, the accused is willing to respond in this way to all your questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will discuss this matter, because I'm not alone in deciding. All of the Judges will have to give their opinion. I can't give you an immediate answer but we would also have to hear the position of the Prosecution. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I appreciate the last comment because we, the Prosecution, would certainly want to be heard on that topic. But I can preview -- I think it's fair to say that I can preview our position by saying that we would oppose such a practice as being totally contrary to existing practice at this institution over the past 15 years; but if a written application is filed, then we will certainly respond, make a written response to it. Your Honour, I rise to my feet primarily on another matter. Since it relates to the next witness. Since the weekend, we have reviewed the 92 ter statement for Mr. Kvesic proposed by the Praljak Defence. It is 11 pages long, Your Honours, and would plainly require the Praljak Defence to engage in well more, I'm sure, given the history in this courtroom, well more than an hour of examination if it was conducted, if it was taken viva voce. The Chamber will also recall that the established practice in this case that where a -- one party tenders a witness's evidence on paper by 92 ter, the opposing party is given substantially more time for cross-examination than the time it takes to simply introduce a statement. In reviewing the 11-page statement of Mr. Kvesic, the Prosecution estimates that it will require at least an hour to cross-examine Mr. Kvesic on that statement alone. Therefore, we are requesting that, in addition to the time allowed for cross-examination in response to the Stojic evidence, that then when Mr. Kvesic is taken by the Praljak Defence, the Prosecution will need an hour to cross-examine him on that statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may only briefly respond. [Interpretation] I -- when considering this request by the OTP for additional time in examining witness Kvesic who is testifying under Rule 92 ter, I see no explanation as to why, what this is based on. The statement is not long, the witness will be questioned as Mr. Stojic's Defence witness in direct, and I see no need. And secondly, there is a practical issue because according to plan, the witness should have -- is supposed to complete his testimony tomorrow. As I told you, I will only put the formal questions required to have the 92 ter statement admitted, and there will be just a few more questions because I met the witness this morning and a piece of information came up which I find very important, but this will take three or four minutes at the most. So in total it will take five or six minutes. Therefore, I consider that my learned friend should put forward the real reasons, the real meat of his request so that we can see what it's actually about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm really quite surprised by counsel's position on this. This is not even a close question. We've had almost three years of trial in which the established practice has been when a 92 ter statement is tendered, which can be tendered in a matter of a couple of minutes, Is this your statement, witness, is it your signature, boom, boom, boom, can be done in one minute. There's 11 pages of text. You can't say that cross-examination is limited to the same amount of time to tender the statement nor has the Chamber ever, ever done so. So what Mr. Kovacic says is just simply unfounded, with great respect. Now, the Prosecution is asking for a meaningful time to examine an 11-page statement if it was tendered viva -- and we have no problem with tendering pursuant to 92 ter. Of course, the Prosecution has done the same; other Defence counsel will do the same. But when you tender evidence in that way, the opposing party must be given an opportunity for meaningful cross-examination which obviously takes longer than simply tendering the statement. And that's our position. It's nothing new. The Chamber has followed this procedure many times in the past three years and it's very obvious why. You can't have a cross -- meaningful cross-examination in two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, I really apologise. [Interpretation] I may not have spoken precisely enough or I may have misunderstood my learned friend. I understood him to be asking additional time, additional to the proportion we were always granted, because Your Honours always worked out an estimate as to how long such a statement would take had it been introduced in live testimony. So I may have misunderstood. I thought that my learned friend was asking time in addition to this time and for that I see no reason. But there's just one point I think should be made here. The OTP received this statement in the Croatian language, Dr. Kvesic's statement, a few days after we filed the 62 ter list. They received it in English, I think, in January of this year. Therefore, I don't see any reason to refer to the length of the statement or shortage of time because they've evidently had enough time to prepare. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, the witness is a witness for the Stojic Defence so let us not pollute, so to speak, the Stojic Defence with a 72 ter list which would enable the Prosecutor to -- rather, a 92 ter list which would enable the OTP to question in all directions. I don't understand why you are not just asking that this statement be admitted under 92 bis. Perhaps there's no particular value in doing so. Perhaps if the witness is coming to corroborate certain aspects, why don't you just admit it under 92 bis. And as regards, Mr. Scott, who always wants a lot of time, I remember that in the Krajisnik case, Mr. Karadzic came and it was a public testimony, everyone followed it, and I watched the screen, like everybody else, to see how the 92 ter procedure functions. Mr. Karadzic prepared a very long document, several dozens of pages, and at the time, the Appeals Chamber stated that Mr. Karadzic had one hour and the OTP one hour. No more. So you've been talking about longer time and I'm a bit surprised, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the records in this case are quite clear that the party in this trial, and I mean everyone, including the Judges, of recent months, the party in this trial that takes the least amount of time is the Prosecution. The Registrar's time records indicate that, so I have no reason to offer any apology on behalf of the Prosecution for its use of the time. We use less time than anyone else in the courtroom, so it's -- I have to make that point clear, Your Honour, with the greatest of respect. Now, what we said was, what we asked was, that in this -- for this witness, in addition to whatever other time would be allocated, that we would have it -- for the cross-examination of the Praljak portion of the evidence, that we would have an hour. So whatever the original time was, it's our estimate that in reviewing the 11-page statement that's what we will take -- that's what it will take in total as to that part of the evidence, not concerning the Stojic case, concerning the Praljak evidence. That's our request, Your Honour. Of course the Chamber -- it will be in the Chamber's hands, but that's our request based upon a review and assessment of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to know whether I have misunderstood something or not, because it seems to me that there is not really a contradiction between what Mr. Scott says and what Mr. Kovacic said. Mr. Scott opened this part of his point by saying that this, the subject matter covered by this declaration would take about one hour to extract in direct examination, and therefore, he was asking for one hour for cross-examination, and that is what the Chamber has practiced so far. So I think we do not even have a dispute but we will, of course, deliberate in the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. If I can just -- if I can just clarify a couple of things in passing on this point. I do just need to briefly respond. Counsel has indicated that we received the statement sometime ago and therefore shouldn't need the time to -- for cross-examination. That's a complete disconnect. When we received the statement, whether we received it yesterday or two months from now, has nothing to do with the amount of time necessary to put the question to the witness in court, so that's simply a complete non sequitur. Secondly, Your Honour, we do have these specific requests because so far we haven't received this information. I don't know if an exhibit number -- typically what happens is an exhibit number is given for the 92 ter statement in advance so that that can be used, or we can use the e-court version if that hasn't -- can't be accomplished, but normally that's been done prior to the appearance of the witness. So we'd either like to have an exhibit number or just confirmation that it is the e-court version that will be used so we can make our final preparations. Secondly, Your Honour, Mr. Kovacic made reference a few moments ago to something -- learning -- having learned something very important from the witness. We are sure, of course, that we'll receive advance notice by further disclosure of that prior to the witness coming into the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell Mr. Kovacic the following thing. Mr. Kovacic, on several occasions you have presented us with 92 ter versions and I think you have several of those. When the Chamber determined the time allocation for you, we decided on the time we were going to allocate you on the basis of the 65 ter list. Now, if you are going to use this other technique and say such and such a witness, 92 ter witness, what is the consequence of that going to be? OTP is going to say, Well, if this was done viva voce, I would have taken one hour. Now, on that basis, OTP will be accumulating hours and hours, whereas you will have very little time since you are keeping your time for other witnesses. And I've already said this because I initiated that article of 92 ter, there's an excessive use of 92 ter, that's quite clear. That is the problem. So if you take twenty 92 ter witnesses and you say, I need two minutes and I'm going to present the 20 statements, they all have 10 or 15 pages, that's going to take you 10 times two minutes, 20 minutes, and OTP will have 50 hours. Now that is a real problem. The Judges will reflect on this, and we'll be informing you of their decision. This is by no means a minor issue because it has huge repercussions on the length of the trial. So if there's nothing else to say, we shall stop there. Ms. Nozica, I think you wanted to say something else. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't respond because there's no point in embarking of this whole discussion, but I do want to put it on record so that it can be given some thought. I believe that in the system we have in this courtroom what is happening is the allocation of a certain number of hours for presenting the Defence case. You have given us a certain quota, and whether we are happy with it or not, we must fit in. On the other hand, I think it is the absolute right of the Defence to decide whether to call a witness as a viva voce witness or whether it considers it can put up with the damage caused by calling a witness as a 92 ter witness, because you will agree with me that such testimonies are less effective, but we have to put up with that, or whether we will call a witness as a 92 bis and not bring him here at all. The Defence can decide that on its own. But I have to say the following: If a witness is going to testify in any case because he has been called by another Defence team, I cannot put him forward as a 92 bis several months later for more than one reason. First of all, I don't know what stance the OTP will take, I don't know how Your Honours will deal with this. You can reject my suggestion that he be called so I think that 92 bis should be more restrictive than 65 ter because the OTP can cross-examine. Whether a ten-page statement is worth one hour or two hours or half an hour, that is for Your Honours, as professionals, to decide. Whatever you decide will probably be all right. I won't go into it. But please leave us the freedom, which I feel we are entitled to, to choose for ourselves in what form we will call a witness. As a live witness, as a 92 bis or a 65 ter. Of course we must carefully plan for each such witness. This particular witness, Dr. Kvesic, I think should be a 92 ter witness, especially as there is a question which cropped up in the interview, and I do apologise to my learned friend for not having submitted this information yet. I only received it at noon today and I've just started. I had already started writing an e-mail to tell him about it. It's not a long topic and it won't be difficult. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, we have given a decision on this question of time and I'm rather surprised that you should come back and question this decision of the Chamber. In the oral decision which I have here before me, it was stated that there will be the examination-in-chief of this witness for one hour, that the other Defence counsels will have 30 minutes, that Mr. Praljak will have 20 minutes to present his 92 ter. That the other Defence counsels will have 15 minutes, and that OTP will have 30 minutes. This was decided upon. This was an oral decision given by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for that. The only thing that any party can do is make its request to the Chamber based upon our assessment of that statement and that's all we've done. Of course I'm in the Chamber's hands. If the Chamber does not give us the time that we request, that's, of course, a decision the Chamber can make. All we can do is rise to our feet and make the request with great respect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please. Microphone please, says the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was saying that my colleague is getting impatient. Mr. Coric. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: Your Honour, I'll be very brief, but I had to rise to my feet in the interest of the Coric Defence because I don't agree with certain matters that were stated by Mr. Kovacic and this is what it is about. I share the concern with Judge Antonetti with respect to 92 ter statements and the time allotted for cross-examination after that. Now, I differ from Mr. Kovacic because I remember the time allotted during the Prosecution case when the Prosecution entered under 92 ter statements also some ten pages, or perhaps a little shorter, and took about ten minutes to do that, and I asked several times just a few more minutes for my cross-examination and I was told that the rule is quite clear and that the economy of the proceedings were paramount and I was given just two minutes. That's why I don't agree with Mr. Kovacic when he says that previously the principle was different in allotting time. I do believe that it can happen to any party that they need more time for a particular witness when you see the statement, but then that they have to say what parts of the statement, what it's about and what it is that is necessary if the Trial Chamber to gain the right impression. It would turn out this way that the Prosecutor needs more time for a 92 ter statement or, rather, equal time as viva voce required by Ms. Nozica. So I don't agree with that. Secondly, and I wasn't able to get to my feet earlier on, you just asked the Prosecutor with respect to Mr. Praljak's testimony. I understand the desire of Mr. Praljak and I don't doubt that he wants to present the truth in this courtroom as soon as possible, but also what can happen is that in presenting that truth, the interests of some of the other accused in this courtroom are violated. And so if you were to permit that motion, then we would have to re-assess all the time spent by Mr. Praljak in saying things in court, and then all of us together, including the Prosecutor, would ask for more time for cross-examination. I think that that is not feasible. I understand everybody's goodwill and everybody's desires and wishes but I think that impractical technically speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, we must come to a stop now. We shall meet again tomorrow afternoon, 2.15 -- sorry, Mr. Scott. I didn't see you. You are hidden behind a pillar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise for being hidden, Your Honour. It's one of the disadvantages of this courtroom. Sorry for that. Your Honour, sorry, but if I could have two more minutes just to be clear on this. The -- Mr. President, you quite properly just reminded me of the Trial Chamber's prior ruling that the Praljak Defence would get upon -- for direct examination purposes would get 20 minutes and the Prosecution would get 20 minutes for cross. With the greatest, respect that really makes the very point that we are making. It has not been the past practice of the Chamber to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mistake, you get 30 minutes, not 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 30 minutes. Thank you, Your Honour. It has been not been the past practice of the Chamber to act with that kind of close amount of time, with the greatest respect. It is -- what Mr. Kovacic gets to do is put in a written statement and gets 20 minutes. We don't get a written statement and we get 10 minutes more to conduct a cross-examination. That's why we've asked the Chamber, and if the Chamber wants to consider our request to be a request for reconsideration so be it. I think it's completely fitting with past practice that when a witness is tendered through 92 ter, and we can have a wider discussion about 92 ter in the future, and I have also my own views on the practice, but, nonetheless, the established practice has been the opposing party is given a fair chance at meaningful cross-examination and is not measured so closely by the amount of time given to the party tendering the statement. I just wanted the record to be clear on that. I thank you for the extra minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, as far as I understood you, Mr. Kovacic will be using two minutes, you will be getting 30 minutes. 15 times more than he will. So the Chamber will discuss this once again and see whether we shall continue with our previous decision or whether there will be a change. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: One small correction. It is really two, three minutes, for all formalities, but I will have additional question to the witness since he -- I bump to one issue which need clarification. But it is -- again, I cannot make a promise, but it is maybe three, four minutes maximum. So really not considerable time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I tried to get to my feet several times. I'd just like to ask all parties who are to decide the time to try to complete the witness tomorrow because he has additional obligations and responsibilities, so I don't know if he can stay on until Thursday. But, Your Honour, this is a perfect illustration as to how difficult it to plan Defence time. You say bring in two or three witnesses. Until 15 minutes ago, I was absolutely certain that we'd get through the witness tomorrow, but now I'm not so sure. So, all these problems that we have to face because it's live. Decisions are changed as we go along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why I asked you to get the witness here today and you told me that you couldn't do that. So I had anticipated this problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for seeing to that, but I wasn't able to physically. If you can understand that. Physically, I was unable to finish with one witness one day and hold a proofing session with another to preparing to come into court the next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We meet again tomorrow at quarter past 2.00. I hope the electricity supply will be up and running. There was a problem today, as you well know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of February, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.48 p.m.,
